We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.
Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back , circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China . This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.
What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.
A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.
Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.
Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.
And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.
Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.
It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.
So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.
Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.
It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”
So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.
Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.
Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.
Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.
Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”
A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons.
One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.
The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”
Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine , Gaza , and Sudan.
According to NPR , Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.
It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.
Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.
For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.

For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.
The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.
Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”
Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.
Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.
The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.
This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.
In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”
Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”
But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?
Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.
Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.
A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”
Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”
How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.
A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”
For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.
Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.
“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”
Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen ), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor.
Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid.
Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”
Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”

Director Takashi Yamazaki ups the ante by pitting Godzilla against one of the monster’s greatest foes
It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.
(Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.
Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.
Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero .
Godzilla Minus Zero is set two years after the events of the first film, with Kamiki and Hamabe reprising their roles as Kōichi and Noriko, along with Nagatani as Akiko. The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country. Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction. Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah , whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers.
It isn’t long before Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka)—i.e., the dude with the magnificent wavy gray hair who is director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau—seeks out Kōichi for help in dealing with this new kaiju threat. His team is able to track Ghidorah’s movements via electrical storms and other pertinent weather patterns, thanks to meteorologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa). But the team has no idea how they might defeat this new threat to life and infrastructure. It’s hardly a spoiler to note that at some point, a regenerated Godzilla will come into play.
(WARNING: significant spoilers appear below. Stop reading now if you haven’t seen the film.)
Yamazaki has retained the visual tone that made the film’s predecessor so striking; it feels like classic Godzilla fare of yore, just with 21st century cutting-edge visual effects. If anything, he’s upped his game on the special effects front, reflecting the larger production budget he had to work with. (It’s also the first Japanese movie filmed specifically for IMAX and it’s well-worth seeing in that format.)
Much of that budget went toward bringing the central monsters to cinematic life, and Godzilla Minus Zero does not disappoint. Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground. And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution.
Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield : Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general. Granted, it occurs in a dream sequence of biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), who survived the Hiroshima blast that killed his wife and children and longs for revenge. And it’s not just indulgence on the director’s part: the scene reinforces the traditional theme of linking Godzilla to nuclear radiation and the horrors of the atomic bomb.
Nor does Yamazaki ignore the human factor via the dilemma of his nuclear family trio. Kōichi must wrestle with his conscience: how can he risk his life again to battle a kaiju when it could mean leaving Akiko an orphan yet again should he fail? Noriko is infected with Godzilla’s radioactive G-cells—the only human to survive the mutations in her own body for so long. But her time could be running out, plus they’ve kept her infection secret for fear she will be taken away by the government for experimentation. Sometimes doing the right thing comes at great personal cost, and watching these quite ordinary people grapple with that reality brings emotional depth to the film.
The film ends on a suitably bittersweet note, and while Yamazaki hasn’t dropped any hints about a possible third film in the series, we’d love to learn more about Noriko’s strangely symbiotic connection to Godzilla via the G-cells in her bloodstream. Long may he reign.

The comedian and musician tries not to overthink things and get it done.
You probably know John Roberts best as the voice of Linda Belcher on Bob’s Burgers . The show just wrapped up its 16th season and shows no signs of slowing down anytime soon. The show remains a reliable source of laughs, top-notch puns, and frankly wholesome fun.
Comedy is just part of Roberts’ life, however. In addition to his appearances on Gravity Falls and Comedy Bang! Bang! , he’s also a musician with deep roots in New York City’s queer nightlife scene. He just released his latest record, I Am , on Friday, and it dabbles in ’80s pop, ’90s house, and even dashes of ’00s rave. But while the record sounds made for the dance floor, it actually tackles some pretty heavy subject matter, like mortality, aging, and grief following the loss of his mother.
Despite that, Roberts is still having fun, as you can see in the video for “ Complicated ,” which revels in the queer cult camp of Scorpio Rising , William Friedkin’s Cruising , and The Wolf Man .

We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception.
Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska , making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor.
On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. The governor-elect is also from Alaska, went to Yale, and climbs mountains.
Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most important sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate. This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator. Check this guy out! A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia! But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his.
“The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero. Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied.
Fair enough. If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them. But I’m a journalist. I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped.
So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account.
So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd.

The Anthropic IPO raises big questions about the future of AI, the company’s safety-first mission, and how we balance idealism with capitalism.
Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.
The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.
All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.
You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure , something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first , and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash.

It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people.
Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem.
Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!”
What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it?
I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later.
But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell.
I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good.
So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this.

I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.
Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first?
Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now.
Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that.
Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year.
I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs.
Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work?
They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. Fausto Isidro Meza Flores was one of FBI’s most wanted fugitives and evaded capture for more than a decade
The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that triggered widespread panic in the city of Guasave.
The alleged leader of a major drug-trafficking cartel, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), he had managed to evade arrest for more than a decade, even though there was a reward of up to $5m (£3.8m) on his head.
His FBI “most wanted” poster states his organisation “is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico”.
Mexico’s defence ministry also alleged he is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation, which is allied to the Mayos, one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.
Meza Flores’s alleged second-in-command, Germán N, whose alias is “Serafín”, and José N, an alleged financial operator for the Beltrán Leyva group, were also arrested.
The operation to capture the men was carried out by “elite military forces” with help from US intelligence, according to Mexico’s defence ministry.
After arriving in the “target area … using stealth and surprise”, the ministry said the arresting force came under attack “with gunfire and explosives” but managed to enter a house and make the arrests.
The men were then evacuated to Mexico City on a Mexican air force plane to be handed over to prosecutors.
Videos and photos show civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game at Kuroda Park stadium in Guasave, as well as burnt-out cars.
A barrage of rapid fire from what appeared to be Mexican security force helicopters hit the ground, according to CNN, and players from the Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave teams abandoned the field mid-game.
Four Mexican army infantry soldiers died in the operation, the defence ministry said in a statement posted on X that extended the institution’s condolences to their families.
It added that security forces killed seven attackers and arrested eight alleged criminals in the operation, including three who were transferred to Mexico City and five who were turned over to the attorney general’s office in Culiacán, Sinaloa.
Overnight on Friday the ​military operation triggered a wave of violence in the state of Sinaloa, including armed ‌clashes between Mexican security forces and cartel members, who ‌set up flaming roadblocks in some areas.
By ​Saturday the violence had substantially subsided. Sinaloa state authorities ​said “the situation is under control and being addressed by all levels of government”.
Meza Flores was originally indicted in 2012, and in 2013 the US Treasury placed sanctions on him under the Kingpin Act, freezing his assets.
In 2017, the US Department of State’s Narcotics Rewards Program began offering up to $5m as a reward for information leading directly to his arrest or conviction.
He has been charged with multiple counts of drug-trafficking violations, and use and possession of a firearm in the US, and was wanted in Mexico for organised crime and offences against public health.

Mexican security forces have captured notorious cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, better known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’, in the north-western state of Sinaloa, triggering a wave of violence that sent residents fleeing for safety.
At least 11 people have been killed in violent clashes in Mexico’s Sinaloa state following the capture.
Mexico’s Defense Cabinet said on Saturday afternoon that seven suspected cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers died in a fierce gun battle that broke out on Friday night and continued into the early hours.
Meza Flores, who was among the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was one of eight people arrested during the operation, which was conducted using intelligence provided by the United States.
The arrest took place in Guasave on Friday night, 20 November, during an operation involving Mexican military and security forces. The Mexican government said intelligence provided by the administration of US President Donald Trump had contributed to the operation, although it has not disclosed precisely how the two countries co-operated.
The arrest was followed by armed confrontations, burning vehicles and roadblocks. Disturbing footage circulating on social media showed spectators fleeing in panic as gunfire interrupted a baseball match in Guasave.
According to Mexican authorities, security forces used what they described as ‘stealth and surprise’ to apprehend Meza Flores.
The operation involved specialist units from the Mexican National Guard and Army. Officials said their personnel came under attack from armed individuals using firearms and explosives, believed to be cartel operatives.
Following the exchange of fire, security forces entered a property and arrested Meza Flores, along with other individuals.
The detainees were subsequently evacuated aboard a Mexican Air Force aircraft to Mexico City, according to the authorities.
The Mexican government acknowledged that intelligence supplied by the Trump administration had played a role in locating and capturing the cartel leader. However, officials have so far provided few details about the intelligence-sharing arrangements or the extent of American involvement.
Mexican news outlet N+ also reported that intelligence agencies from Mexico's Defence Ministry and the United States had co-operated in the operation.
The development highlights the importance of intelligence cooperation between Mexico and the United States in tackling organised crime, particularly given the cross-border nature of the drug trade.
The arrest quickly turned into a night of violence in Guasave.
Videos and photographs shared online showed civilians running for cover as gunfire erupted during a baseball match. Spectators could be seen leaving the venue in fear as the situation deteriorated.
Other footage showed vehicles set alight and roads blocked, while armed confrontations reportedly spread beyond the immediate area of the operation.
According to Mexican newspaper La Jornada , the violence included shootings, vehicle fires, roadblocks involving burning lorries and clashes between federal forces and armed groups.
Local authorities urged residents to remain indoors and avoid travelling on affected roads.
The scenes illustrate the immediate risks that major operations against organised crime can pose to civilians living in areas where criminal groups maintain a strong presence.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’, is considered one of Mexico's most significant organised-crime figures.
He is associated with the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation and leads a network also known as the Meza-Flores organisation or the Guasave Cartel.
The group has operated primarily in north-western Mexico, particularly in Sinaloa, and has been linked by US authorities to the trafficking of several illegal drugs, including cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin and marijuana.
Meza Flores rose to prominence following the fragmentation of the Beltrán Leyva organisation and the wider conflicts between rival criminal factions in Mexico.
His organisation has been accused of using violence, intimidation and territorial control to protect its criminal activities.
In February 2025, the FBI placed Meza Flores on its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, underlining the importance US authorities attached to his capture.
The US government had offered a reward of up to US$5 million for information leading to his arrest.
Although the arrest is a major achievement for Mexican security forces, it remains to be seen how it will affect the balance of power between criminal organisations operating in Sinaloa.
The capture of a senior cartel figure does not necessarily mean the dismantling of the organisation he leads. Criminal networks can remain operational following the arrest of their leaders, while rival groups may attempt to exploit any resulting power vacuum.
The immediate unrest highlights the continuing challenges facing the country in its fight against organised crime.

Mexico's military forces captured ​one of the most wanted suspected drug lords, Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," the military announced on Saturday, after a deadly firefight that killed seven suspected attackers and four soldiers. Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was flown to Mexico City after his capture.
Mexico 's military announced on Saturday that it had captured the leader of a drug-trafficking group on the FBI 's list of 10 most wanted fugitives.
Fausto Isidro Meza, alias "Chapo Isidro," and two other leaders of his drug gang were seized by special forces Friday night in in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat announced on X.
The Mexican defence ministry said seven suspected attackers were killed and eight people arrested during the operation, including the three senior gang figures.
Four soldiers sent to reinforce security in the town of Guasave were also killed as gang members mounted fierce resistance to their leader's arrest, it said.
The military seized a .50-caliber rifle, a grenade launcher, grenades, other firearms, drugs and cash. It said there were no reports of civilian casualties.
The operation sparked panic across the surrounding area, with gunfire forcing the suspension of a professional baseball game in Guasave, local media reported.
Unverified videos posted on social media showed people running inside the stadium amid shouts of "Get down, get down!" as bursts of gunfire rang out nearby.
Another video appeared to show a hovering military helicopter firing a machine gun.
Chapo Isidro, 44, is the alleged leader of the Beltran Leyva gang, which is allied with one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel, Mexico's military said.
He was captured alongside his alleged number two and another man identified as a financial operator.
They were transported by a Mexican Air Force aircraft to Mexico City "to be placed at the disposal of the competent prosecutorial authorities," the military said.
After the operation, violence broke out and improvised roadblocks were set up in several areas of Sinaloa, as has occurred following the capture of other recent gang leaders.
The Mexican military said it had launched its anti-blockade plan and was responding with local authorities.
An unverified video circulating on social media overnight appeared to show a detained Chapo Isidro urging his associates to stand down, warning that "children, women, innocent people" could be put in harm's way.
Chapo Isidro faces criminal charges in both Mexico and the United States.
The FBI had placed him on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives, while the US State Department offered a $5 million reward for information leading to his arrest.
Giving his name as Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, the FBI bulletin says his group is responsible for importing "large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States."
His capture comes just days after Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum met on the sidelines of a summit in Asia with US counterpart Donald Trump .
Trump, who has consistently pushed Mexico to do more to tackle drug gangs, said on Friday that they had discussed trade and security in their meeting.
"We're working with her on the cartels because the cartels are running Mexico. I told her that, and we can't let the cartels run Mexico. They're our neighbor," he told reporters at the White House.
The Mexican military said in its post that the operation was conducted "following coordination" with US intelligence in the "framework of bilateral cooperation."
Earlier this year, Sheinbaum faced political pressure over the revelation that US intelligence personnel were operating in the country without her government's approval, following the deaths of two reportedly CIA agents in a road accident.

If Mikel Arteta was delighted to see the back of Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s head coach, the bad news is that another similarly awkward technical area adversary has been installed at St James’ Park.
Arsenal’s manager never seemed to relish trips to face Howe’s old team and he certainly did not enjoy this latest trip to Tyneside, where Matthias Jaissle’s initially overwhelmed team fought back commendably to earn a point courtesy of a stellar second-half performance. At half-time the crowd had felt close to turning against Jaissle but he held his nerve and, thanks to a triple substitution and subtle tactical rejig suggested he is no mug after all.
It left Arsenal – who lost their outstanding goalkeeper David Raya to a potentially significant second-half shoulder injury – still top of the Premier League , six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City, and Arteta with a face like thunder.
Just last week Bruno Guimarães claimed he was “beloved” by Newcastle fans but the club’s former captain turned Arsenal midfielder found himself serenaded by a soundtrack of boos of the sort usually reserved for Sunderland players. Newcastle’s problem is that, despite spending about £275m this summer, they have struggled to replace last season’s departed star trio – Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon.
That reality perhaps left Howe’s successor – who arrived just before the start of the season – making a not so subtle point with his team sheet here. Of Jaissle’s starting XI only the goalkeeper, Lukas Hornicek, the right-back Amar Dedic and the midfielder Sean Steur were close-season signings.
The other five new faces were either benched (Nico González and Matias Fernandez-Pardo) or did not make the 20-man matchday squad (Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Touré). Admittedly Ewen Jaouen is injured but, given Bamba and Toure cost a combined £78.5m, their omission represented quite a statement. Ditto the decision to bench González and Fernandez-Pardo and their individual £50m plus price tag.
Meanwhile the jury remains out on Hornicek. The Czech international has made some excellent saves this season but, initially here, his kicking proved pretty much uniformly poor and he was fortunate to be reprieved after hesitating too long as the impressive Kai Havertz closed in.
Jaissle’s frustration with his goalkeeper proved well apparent as Arsenal took increasing control of a first half that saw Newcastle’s lone striker, William Osula, isolated and even their normally imperious England left-back Lewis Hall given a thorough work out by Noni Madueke.
Much to Arteta’s chagrin, Lewis Miley, preferred to González in the midfield holding role, endeavoured to slow the tempo but the red tide could only be stemmed for so long.
When Havertz dispossessed Hall after the latter miscontrolled a long ball, he cut inside and slid a highly intelligent, beautifully calibrated, pass across to the on-rushing Eberechi Eze. Without breaking stride, Eze exhibited perfect balance and unleashed a gorgeous first-time shot that arrowed, inexorably, past Hornicek.
• Arsenal ended a 21-game run of Premier League games without a draw (W18 D3) since a 2-2 draw with Wolves back in February.
• Since the start of last season, all five of Newcastle’s Premier League draws at St James’ Park have been a 2-2 scoreline.
• Eberechi Eze’s opener for Arsenal (pictured) was his first Premier League goal since April, which also put the Gunners 1-0 ahead against Newcastle. Opta
As the home fans fell eerily silent, Arteta and his staff celebrated a goal sufficiently special to rebuke suggestions that his side are all about efficiency at the expense of artistry these days.
With Declan Rice always available to reinforce his defence and smother any flickering home attack it proved a struggle to recall Newcastle making a meaningful attacking touch inside Arsenal’s box. Fans stationed near the home dugouts told Jaissle what they thought of it all.
Arsenal’s pressing was initially so good that Newcastle were left almost incapable of playing short passes and, instead found themselves reduced to aimless long balls. With Rice and Martin Ødegaard apparently operating on a different midfield planet an equaliser felt like a distant dream.
Yet that seemingly ambitious vision was something Harvey Barnes proved fully capable of buying into. When, early in the second half, Ødegaard made an uncharacteristic error, his heavy touch sliced the ball in Osula’s direction and the Dane played it into Barnes’s path.
All that remained was for the left winger to take a single, steadying, touch before an assured finish left the hitherto redundant David Raya picking his shot out of the net.
Jaissle’s second-half introduction of Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga – all at Newcastle last season – at the expense of Dedic, Steur and Jacob Murphy was paying dividends. Suddenly, almost astonishingly, Arsenal were the team in danger of being pressed into submission.
The home side were closing their guests down far higher up the pitch and had morphed into an infinitely more menacing team. Soon, they were ahead when a Hall corner was headed down by Dan Burn, allowing Malick Thiaw to stab the ball beyond Raya.
Shortly afterwards Arsenal’s goalkeeper was helped off the pitch in evident pain after sustaining a nasty left shoulder injury during an ostensibly benign collision with Osula. On came Kepa Arrizabalaga in a triple substitution also featuring Guimarães’s exit.
Madueke though was still around and he reminded everyone of his presence by meeting the counterattacking Ødegaard’s fine pass, dummying two defenders and watching his slightly deflected shot evade Hornicek’s grasp.
No matter; Jaissle had done enough to win plenty of hearts and minds. Not least the chair, Yasir al-Rumayyan, over from Riyadh to watch his first match of the season and reportedly “take the club’s temperature”.

League leaders Arsenal miss the chance to go eight points clear of second placed Brighton, who play on Sunday.
Arsenal missed the chance to open up an eight-point lead at the top of the Premier League after a stirring second-half fightback from Newcastle held the defending champions to a 2-2 draw .
The Gunners led on Saturday through Eberechi Eze’s strike after a dominant first 45 minutes.
But Mikel Arteta’s men were suddenly headed for defeat when goals from Harvey Barnes and Malick Thiaw provided a much-needed boost for under-fire Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle.
Noni Madueke salvaged a point for Arsenal and stretched their lead at the top over surprise package Brighton to six points.
However, the loss of influential goalkeeper David Raya to injury could provide a twist in the title race that many believed Arsenal would cruise.
Newcastle remain in the bottom half of the table with just one win in six games in all competitions.
Yet, Jaissle can point to his side’s second-half performance as a potential turning point after a difficult start to his reign at St James’ Park.
Arsenal move back six points clear of third-placed Manchester City, but missed the chance to put their foot down in the defence of their title.
Madueke continued his impressive form in the injury absence of Bukayo Saka and hit the post early on.
Former Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes was roundly booed on his first return to Tyneside since making a 75 million pound ($98m) move to the Emirates Stadium in August.
The Brazilian nearly silenced his former faithful when he prodded just wide from a Madueke cross as Arsenal pressed for the opener.
It duly arrived 10 minutes before the break when Kai Havertz pounced on a poor touch by Lewis Hall and brilliantly played in Eze to blast high past Lukas Hornicek.
Jaissle got the response he needed from his half-time team talk as Newcastle came out a completely different proposition after the break.
Arsenal also played a part in letting the home side back into the game and lifting the 50,000 crowd in doing so.
Martin Odegaard shanked his attempt at a long ball forward to allow William Osula to play in Barnes to level.
Suddenly, an Arsenal side that had kept seven clean sheets in their opening 10 league games was on the rocks.
Thiaw bundled home a second for Newcastle just 13 minutes later after Dan Burn was left completely unmarked from a corner and his header was only parried by Raya.
That proved to be one of Raya’s final interventions as the Spaniard had to be replaced by Kepa Arrizabalaga.
Raya would be a massive miss if the Spaniard is sidelined for a significant spell.
But Arsenal regained their composure in time to salvage a point that keeps them well in the driving seat to retain the title.
Odegaard made amends for his earlier error by freeing Madueke down the righ,t and he cut inside before his tame deflected shot found a way past Hornicek.
Madueke told Sky Sports that he thought 2-2 was a “fair” result.
“Game of two halves is fair. First half we were outstanding. Should have got three goals, to be honest. Missed a couple of chances myself. Everything else was there,” he said.
“The second half, the first 20 minutes, was not good by our standard. When you give this team and crowd belief at home, it is difficult. We showed character to get back in the game, but 2-2 is a fair result.”

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.
"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," Trump added.
This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyber-attacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with Trump saying he was not good enough.
Dan Lorhmann, a former analyst for the National Security Agency (NSA), told the BBC News Channel that the NCIC's data included "critical information relating to nationwide criminal activity" and needed to be protected.
He added that while US security agencies including the FBI have "an amazing ability" to keep such information safe" and are "globally respected", the level of cyber-attacks is rising globally.
"There's a lot of different reasons why that's happening but I do have faith in our experts in government," Lorhmann said.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA).
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.

The Finnish Border Guard is leading the operations involving the Sparta II
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.
The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."
After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .
Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.
Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."
No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.
"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.
"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.
"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."
But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

Demonstrations in France and Portugal follow youth-led protests over education and economic hardship across Europe.
Thousands of people have taken to the streets across Europe to protest against rising living costs, unaffordable housing and cuts to public services, as students and workers demand action from their governments.
Demonstrators marched across France and Portugal on Saturday, following youth-led protests in several European countries on Friday.
The gatherings reflect overlapping concerns about economic insecurity, education and future opportunities, although their demands and scale differ considerably between countries.
In France, the Ministry of Interior said 82,500 people joined demonstrations nationwide on Saturday, including 21,500 in Paris, down from 106,000 the previous weekend. Organisers estimated a higher turnout of 150,000.
The protests, now in their sixth consecutive weekend, began in September with students demanding better schools before expanding to include trade unions and the Yellow Vests, a movement that emerged in 2018 over rising fuel prices and living costs.
Demonstrators have also criticised police violence and a new law strengthening protections for officers who use firearms.
In Portugal, thousands marched through Lisbon despite heavy rain, calling for higher wages, affordable housing and relief from rising prices.
The demonstration was organised by CGTP, the country’s largest trade union federation, which also demanded higher pensions and cheaper essential goods.
Portugal’s housing pressures have intensified as property prices have more than doubled since 2017.
Average annual earnings in 2025 were 37 percent below the European Union average, according to the EU’s statistics agency, Eurostat.
The weekend’s demonstrations followed Friday’s youth protests in Germany and Sweden.
About 4,000 people gathered in Berlin, while police reported roughly 200 participants at a Saturday march in Helsinki organised by left-wing and student groups.
Organisers of an international youth strike said demonstrations were planned in at least 25 countries, with demands ranging from greater education funding and climate action to opposition to compulsory military service.
In Germany, the youth campaign Gen Z regelt, meaning “Generation Z takes charge”, announced demonstrations in 73 locations.
In Italy, a nationwide strike organised by the CGIL, one of the country’s main trade union confederations, disrupted transport, schools and some healthcare services on Friday.
Demonstrations took place in more than 100 cities, with union leader Maurizio Landini claiming more than one million participants nationwide.
While some protests were linked through the international youth initiative, others grew out of established national campaigns, bringing different groups onto the streets over concerns about living standards and government spending.
Separately, thousands protested in the Croatian capital, Zagreb, on Saturday over the death of a man at a psychiatric hospital.
Four medical technicians are under investigation on suspicion of aggravated murder.

Report and free match highlights as Newcastle put on a spirited second-half showing to wobble Arsenal, who lost David Raya to a shoulder injury; Noni Madueke equalised to ensure the spoils were eventually shared
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
Arsenal's four-game winning Premier League run without conceding was ended by Newcastle in a frantic 2-2 draw.
For 45 minutes, this looked like another routine victory for Mikel Arteta's winning machine. Arsenal were dominant, controlling the tempo and suffocating Newcastle with their relentless pressure as Eberechi Eze's opener was exactly what the league leaders deserved.
But football showed yet again it's a game of two halves as Matthias Jaissle produced a tactical masterstroke to change the momentum of the game.
The Newcastle boss made a triple substitution that completely transformed the contest. Suddenly, Newcastle were bolder, braver and playing with intensity.
Harvey Barnes sparked the comeback before Malick Thiaw completed a spectacular turnaround on a night when Bruno Guimaraes returned to St James' Park as an Arsenal player but was withdrawn in the second half after a quiet performance. The first Newcastle captain to lift a trophy in 56 years following their historic 2025 Carabao Cup triumph, he was cheered at full-time when he completed a lap of the pitch.
Arsenal were rattled after falling behind. And their afternoon took another worrying turn when goalkeeper David Raya was forced off with a shoulder injury.
Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta said: "Unfortunately, he had to come off which is never good news. He will get assessed now and probably he will have an MRI tomorrow [Sunday] to see what it is exactly because at the moment I don't know. It was a knock.
"I don't know how it happened and what the injury is at the moment, so we have to wait and see tomorrow."
But champions find a way to respond and Noni Madueke delivered the equaliser to ensure they escaped Tyneside with a point that extended their lead at the top of the table to six points over second-placed Brighton, who could halve the deficit at Hull on Sunday.
"My feeling is that we lost two points today. We were exceptional in the first half. At every level. Our intensity, the clarity that we have, how to attack the jumps of Newcastle every time they wanted to go man-to-man, the composure that we have, the way we use our relationship to break their press. And it should have been 2-0, 3-0 or 4-0 up, clear.
"But it wasn't. And when it wasn't, then we expected in the second half that we have to again raise the level because the opponent is going to have a reaction. And the opponent did have a reaction and we were very below the level that is required to stretch the gap in a game like this in this stadium. And then we gave them belief.
"And I say we give them belief because we give them a goal, we give them a throw-in that we just give them the ball. We have no structure to control the opposite winger. We concede a goal and it's game on.
"From that it became a very chaotic game. Every set-piece, we know that they are exceptional at it and we concede from a set-piece.
"Then you have to react. And then we went back to the exceptional team that we were in the first half again for another 25 minutes and we scored a great goal. We create infinity of openings to create and score the third goal, but we lack some time or to be precise, to make that count."
"A big, big point. When you feel the momentum in the second half, then you're almost feeling it's two points lost. But staying humble and seeing the big picture over 90 minutes, I think it's a fair result and something we can carry on and build on.
"We tried to encourage the players. Tactically, it was not too much of a difference. Honestly, it's just about believing in being front-footed, being aggressive, doing the last steps and believing also in your teammates. We need to use the momentum and that's what the lads did in the second half playing really vertical and using the gaps and the space and that was done with success.
"You see what's possible, especially at home with our fans - an unbelievable atmosphere, the energy was giving me goosebumps.
"This needs to be the standard. This unity, players and the fans and then the playing style. It's how we want to do that. The synergy should thrive us and give us confidence that we can do much better in the future."
